query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Switching from conventional thermal-spray to an optimized cold spray deposition process will increase the FeCoNiCrAl bond coat thickness beyond the feedstock-limited 15–45 μm range while preserving coating integrity and limiting as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy powder feedstock (15–45 μm) used in conventional thermal-spray deposition that produces coatings with insufficient thickness and some oxidation.
generation.intervention: Adopt cold spray deposition with optimization of particle velocity to maximize particle impact energy.
generation.conditions: Deposition performed under conditions typical for bond coats in thermal barrier coating systems (i.e., minimal thermal input, controlled atmosphere to limit oxygen exposure) and subsequently used in high-temperature environments (such as aero-engine components).
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced particle kinetic energy promotes a denser, mechanically interlocked coating buildup while the low-temperature process minimizes in-flight oxidation, preserving the original BCC phase of the HEA.
generation.mechanism: Increasing particle velocity in cold spray enhances the impact momentum, enabling better particle deposition and buildup to overcome the thickness shortfall. Simultaneously, the cold spray process reduces thermal exposure that normally causes oxidation during conventional thermal spraying.
generation.predicted_outcome: The cold-sprayed coating will exhibit a statistically significant increase in thickness (beyond the 15–45 μm baseline) while maintaining a homogeneous microstructure with minimal oxide inclusions, thereby preserving coating integrity.
generation.baseline: Bond coats produced from 15–45 μm feedstock using conventional thermal-spray methods, which do not achieve the desired coating thickness and incur measurable oxidation.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness may depend on feedstock quality and the precise optimization of particle velocity; extreme substrate geometries or non-ideal gas conditions may limit the generalizability of the results.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal range of particle velocities for achieving the desired thickness and minimal oxidation in FeCoNiCrAl coatings needs further tuning. Variations in powder morphology and process scale-up effects introduce additional uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled study comparing two deposition methods on identical FeCoNiCrAl substrates: a conventional thermal-spray process and an optimized cold spray process. Systematically vary the particle velocity in the cold spray process while keeping all other parameters constant. Post-deposition, measure coating thickness, microstructural integrity, and oxidation levels.
measurements: Phase composition and microstructure (using XRD and SEM)
Adhesion strength between coating and substrate (via standard adhesion tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cold-sprayed coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in thickness compared to the conventional thermal-sprayed baseline, or if they show similar or higher as-sprayed oxidation levels and compromised coating integrity, the hypothesis is falsified.

For example, both as-cast AlSiTiCrFeCoNiMo0.5 and AlSiTiCrFeNiMo0.5 are dual-phase alloys (BCC + FCC); however, if fabricated via thermal spray, they have only the supersaturated BCC solid solution []. Cold-sprayed AlFeNiCoCr alloy retains the same BCC structure as was observed in the powder []. In contrast, in the plasma-sprayed coating of the same composition, the FCC phase is observed as the major one []. reading.lever: Switch to cold spray deposition with optimized particle velocity to enhance coating buildup.
reading.why: Cold spray minimizes oxidation while improving deposition efficiency, directly addressing the thickness shortfall for FeCoNiCrAl bond coats.
